{{nihongo|'''Ōhi Shrine'''|意富比神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Shimōsa Province]].

==Origin of company name==
There are various theories about the origin of the company's name, ``Ohhi, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Old kana usage}}: Ohohi. The main ones are shown below.
* The theory that he is a food god, meaning a great fire or a great meal.
* The theory is that it is a sunset because it is located on a hill that is directly facing the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=sunset}} sun.
* Theory that the {{ill|Ujigami|Q767655|qid=Q767655}} of the {{ill|Ō clan|Q11430816|qid=Q11430816|lt=Yitomi}}, an ancient and powerful ruling family.
* This theory, which means Dainichi, is Otendo-sama (sun god), which {{ill|Peasant|Q838811|qid=Q838811}} in this region had originally worshiped.{{efn|This theory was announced as a theory that added criticism and research to the previous theories, and attracted attention. As if to support this theory, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Tendo Nenbutsu}} has been popular in the city since ancient times, and Daijingu Shrine also has a hanging Buddha statue representing the ``Dainichi Nyorai statue'' that was used before the {{ill|Shinto Buddhism Order|qid=Shinto Buddhism Order|lt=Separation of Shinto and Buddhism}} order was issued. }}

== History ==
According to the shrine's legend, it began in the year 40 of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|Q329723|qid=Q329723}}, when {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Nihon Takeru}} prayed for the pacification of the eastern region during his expedition to the east. At that time, the local residents were suffering from drought, and when Nihon Takeru prayed for rain at the same time, it was said that it started raining. Originally, the local sun god ``Itobijin (Dainichijin)'' was enshrined at the company, and it attracted the faith of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=fishermen}} in the surrounding area ({{ill|Tokyo Bay|Q141017|qid=Q141017}}). The first time I read {{ill|Rikkokushi|Q1151168|qid=Q1151168|lt=Kokushi}} is in "{{ill|Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku|Q1052981|qid=Q1052981}}" (Japan)|Q1075635|Jōkan}}5 years ({{ill|863|Q25052|qid=Q25052}}) In the article dated May 26, {{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}, it is listed as a small shrine.Later, this area was donated to {{ill|Ise Grand Shrine|Q687168|qid=Q687168}} and {{ill|mikuriya|Q11488831|qid=Q11488831}} ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Natsumi Mikuriya}}), and Shinmeisha Shrine, which enshrines Amaterasu Omikami, the deity of Ise Grand Shrine, as its guardian, is now {{jalink|Hie Shrine} in {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Natsumidai}}. (Natsumidai, Funabashi City) ||Hie Shrine}} However, with the decline of Mikuriya, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Shinmeisha}} also became obsolete and was enshrined at Ifuhi Shrine. After that, faith in {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Amaterasu no Omikami}} became stronger, and the name of Ifuhi Shrine was gradually forgotten, and it came to be called exclusively Funabashi Shinmei or Funabashi Daijingu. Until the Sengoku period, the powerful {{ill|Chiba clan|Q2975237|qid=Q2975237}} family {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Tomi clan}}, who maintained power in this area, served as {{ill|Gūji|Q11453500|qid=Q11453500}}. Even now, he has changed his surname to Chiba, and members of the same family serve as {{ill|Gūji|Q11453500|qid=Q11453500}}.

The shrine held many medieval documents, including the {{jalink|Ichikawa-Funabashi War|Q812} from the Boshin War that occurred during the {{ill|Meiji Restoration|Q8707|qid=Q8707}}. 56|Battle of Funabashi}} It was burnt down along with the shrine building, and only a few items remain today, including letters from Mitsutane Chiba and a document dating back many years called ``Funabashi Mikuriya Rokuga Goda Kazunoji.'' The main hall was rebuilt in 1896, and the worship hall was rebuilt in 1891. In 1872, it was elevated to the status of a prefectural shrine, and the name was restored to Ifuhi Shrine as recorded in the Engishiki Shinmyocho.It was revered by the imperial court and the shogunate, and members such as {{ill|Taira no Masakado|Q1207652|qid=Q1207652}}, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800|qid=Q242800}}, and {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|Q171977|qid=Q171977}} donated shrine territories and built and renovated the shrine buildings. At Tokiwa Shrine in the grounds of the shrine, a wooden Ieyasu statue containing Ieyasu's tooth is enshrined. In modern times, successive emperors such as {{ill|Emperor Meiji|Q174231|qid=Q174231}}, {{ill|Emperor Taishō|Q157052|qid=Q157052}}, and {{ill|Hirohito|Q34479|qid=Q34479}} have visited the shrine.

== Rank salary ==
* {{ill|863|Q25052|qid=Q25052}} (Jōkan 5th year) {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Junior Fifth Rank Lower}} confers {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Seigoi Lower}}
* {{ill|871|Q24754|qid=Q24754}} (13th year of Jogan) {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Senior Fifth Rank Upper}} awarded
* {{ill|874|Q23843|qid=Q23843}} (16th year of Jogan) Awarded {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Junior Fourth Rank Lower}} {{efn|{{ill|Nara period|Q189178|qid=Q189178}}, systems regarding {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Jingi}} and {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=rituals}} were put in place, and he began to receive generous protection from the Ritsuryo state. Also, from this time the custom (shakaku) of conferring official rank on gods (shrines) arose. According to records, Honsha was awarded the rank of 4th rank in the 16th year of the Jogan era. This effectively means that he was ranked higher than the fifth rank, which was appointed as {{ill|Shimōsa Province|Q1053695|qid=Q1053695}}{{ill|Kokushi (official)|Q1351234|qid=Q1351234}}, and shows that the head office was positioned as an important shrine at that time. However, there is no clear reason why he was given such a high rank. However, it is generally believed that they were trying to increase the influence of {{ill|Yamato Kingship|Q2658252|qid=Q2658252|lt=Yamato Dynasty}} by bestowing a high rank on the headquarters, which was highly worshiped by the residents of this region. }}

== Event ==

== Dedicated Sumo at Funabashi Daijingu Shrine (October 20th) ==
The votive {{ill|Sumo|Q40561|qid=Q40561}} held as an annual autumn festival has a long history, originating from {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|Q171977|qid=Q171977}}'s Kanran sumo held in {{ill|1590|Q6764|qid=Q6764}} ({{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|Q1145058|qid=Q1145058}}18). At that time, Ieyasu occasionally held falconry events in Shimousa, and had an annex set up as a lodging in {{ill|Funabashi|Q271417|qid=Q271417|lt=Funabashi}}. ({{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Funabashi Goten}} was located in what is now {{ill|Funabashi|Q271417|qid=Q271417}} Honmachi 4-chome, and was called "Gotenji." The former site is {{ill|Funabashi-tōshōgū|Q11614238|qid=Q11614238}}) One day, Ieyasu saw a child playing sumo. It is said that the origin of sumo is said to have been dedicated to Funabashi Daijingu Shrine, where people were deeply religious, and later on, {{ill|Kanjin|Q6363447|qid=Q6363447}} himself became the origin of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=amateur sumo}}.Amateur sumo in Jingu is known for attracting strong wrestlers, and it still contributes to the training of {{ill|Rikishi|Q2727289|qid=Q2727289}} from {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Tokatsu}}. Also, until recently, it was famous for the gathering of enthusiastic {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=spectators}}, including {{ill|Fisherman|Q331432|qid=Q331432}}, and spectators dissatisfied with the decisions would throw things and {{jal It was said that there was a scene where ink|Gyoji|Q907647}} was beaten up and he clashed with {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=young people}} wearing {{ill|Manju|Q11353895|qid=Q11353895}}, which caused a lot of excitement.
